examples.title: Loops & branches
examples.lesson: At -O0, Ghidra recovers an almost exact `for` loop, `% 2` included. At -O1 the `% 2` becomes a bit test (`& 1`) and the counter changes shape: x86-64 indexes the array, ARM64 walks a pointer and counts down. At -O2 the loop is vectorized to handle many numbers per iteration, and the same logic ends up buried under dozens of temporaries.

examples.title: Structs
examples.lesson: Field names don't survive compilation. All the binary keeps are byte offsets like +0x14, +0x18 and +0x20. Once you define the struct, `*(float *)(param_1 + 0x18)` turns back into `p->health`. From -O1 on, `if (score >= 0) alive++` also becomes the branch-free `alive - (~score >> 31)`.

examples.title: Recursion
examples.lesson: At -O0 the function calls itself. From -O1 on, the compiler has turned the recursion into a plain loop, and -O2 unrolls that loop: 8 multiplies per pass on x86-64, 4 running products on ARM64. The decompiler can only show what's in the binary, not what you originally wrote.

examples.title: Strings & imports
examples.lesson: Stripping removes your own function names, but calls into shared libraries (`_strlen`, `_strcmp`) and string literals ("hunter2") stay readable at every optimization level. Reverse engineers usually start from these.

examples.title: Switch statements
examples.lesson: On x86-64, clang compiles this `switch` to a jump table (an array of offsets plus one indirect `jmp`), and Ghidra rebuilds the `switch` from it. On ARM64 it emits a chain of compares at -O0 and branch-free `csel` trees once optimized. Same source, completely different shape, and the decompiler shows whichever one is actually in the binary.
